title: The Mountain and the Dwelling of God
english: Not a mountain, but the house of God; for this is interpreted as Bethel, which is not only [a house] but also with other things according to what was said in Aisma: 'My brother is like a deer or a young hart upon the mountains of Bethel' (Gen 25:9). For many mountains and hills are in the house of God, as from 'Behold, this one comes leaping upon the mountains, fleeing upon the hills' (Ps 42:6); and with each progress there is to ascend to a hill, and from the hill to a mountain, and from lower mountains to higher ones; for this is known both in the introductions of virtues and in the virtues themselves.

But there is one mountain above all, the Savior and Lord of us, concerning whom it is said: 'The mountain of the Lord shall be made manifest at the latter end of the days' (Zech 14:4), which is another thing compared to the other mountains, so as to speak for the sake of the holy teaching, so that no one might misunderstand: 'Why do you suppose [it is] fortified mountains?' Then, teaching the most excellent mountain, he says: 'The mountain of God, a fertile mountain, a fortified mountain, a fertile mountain. Why do you suppose [it is] fortified mountains, the mountain in which God was pleased to dwell?' which signifies the Lord having become man. For the incarnation is shown through this word, just as also with Job: 'Did you not care for me like milk, and did you not curdle me like cheese?' (Job 10:10). For the Savior alone [comes] from a virgin; therefore it is said. Is this said concerning others? For no one else had such a constitution. Therefore Job did not say 'I was curdled,' but 'You curdled me like cheese'; for what the Spirit has done, the casting of the seed in others works by the command of God. And the same 'fertile' exists from the presence of the Spirit and from the power of the Most High.

And in the common sense, all and even the temple of the Savior are by creation from God, but [the Savior is] exceptional through the Lord; for He has used it as an instrument toward the incarnation. And just as all the earth of God is a creation, but the temple had [it] exceptional because of the God being honored there, so also regarding the things previously mentioned. And since, wherever God honors, that place is called His house, Jacob testifies saying: 'How fearful is this place! This is nothing else but the house of God, and this is a gate of heaven' (Gen 28:17). Therefore one must not pay attention, if [he] says...

Many will call themselves Christs according to what is said: 'Many will come in my name, saying, I am the Christ' (Matthew 24:5). For there is a mountain in which God pleased to dwell; for the pleasure of the dwelling was not made by any man. Therefore, Abram, advancing through the intellect, burns toward this mountain.

Indeed, coming without neglect, he testified to him, saying: 'Your father Abraham rejoiced in order to see my day, and he saw and rejoiced' (John 8:56), having been enlightened by the true light being presented to him from the preceding advancements. And it is also good to say that this mountain is 'toward the east'; for it has lights from every side. Whatever conception of this mountain you take, it is luminous; for it is called wisdom, word, life, truth, justice, sanctification, and redemption. All these things, while rising, are lights—not many lights according to their essence, for they have one underlying subject, the Son of God—but diverse according to their energies.

Therefore, 'toward the east' of the house of God, which shines through all, the holy man came, being led by virtues; and it is also possible to call the various doctrines of piety 'eastings,' through which Abraham had arrived at the tent, which he used for the advancements—for this tent signifies the house of God being permanent; for 'I will pass through a place of wondrous habitation until the house of God' (Psalm 84:10). Having passed through the tent, he presses into the house that remains forever, with which there is no other ascent. This is also said in another psalm: 'How beloved are your habitations, Lord of powers! My soul longs and even faints for the courts of the Lord' (Psalm 84:2).

For he who has not yet reached the courts, while in the tents, has love advancing and expects completion in saying: 'My heart and my flesh shall rejoice in a living God' (Psalm 36:9), when it occurs in that establishment, with which there is no other, into which those who have reached are called blessed, the psalmist saying: 'Blessed are all those dwelling in your house' (Psalm 84:4), not as sojourners but as dwellers; for this belongs to those in tents and advancements, but to dwell is to come into the house of God, in which they are blessed, as it were 'unto the ages of ages,' praising him.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Altar of Virtue and Calling upon the Lord
english: Above all things the end is evident: that for which the tent has been pitched, having advanced through progress and remaining toward perfection, and for which the one persuaded by the word, despite being dissuaded, will arrive: 'Watch your foot, lest when you go into the house of God and draw near, you hear' (Ps 119:10). For thus he will be able to dwell in the house, saying, 'That I may dwell in the house of the Lord for length of days' (Ps 27:4). It must be known that through these things the divine citizenship is symbolically shown, even if the persona of Abraham is not yet fully completed, for he has not yet been called away.

And he pitches the tent 'by the sea,' being firm and unshakeable because of holding fast to virtue perfectly, so as to say: 'Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution?' (Rom 8:35) and the following, regarding which he says 'sea,' would not be sins. For whenever a saint is, even in perfection, he has a dizziness pressing upon him and the instability of created nature, which the perfect man, as a charioteer, prevents from the activity of evil by remaining in its power, which is blessed; for this is good even while existing in virtue, since even the evil man exists in the power of virtue, having turned to this by his own intention, though he did not guard himself as one who has become good.

And he himself also pitches the tent 'in winds from the south' in a way suitable to reaching the mountain of the house of God and being illuminated through all things from the east, which are the virtues according to their kind, and making no care for any of the opposing things—for even the waves from the sea do not overturn his well-established structure—which transforms the words of Jesus into works by becoming a feast; for this is interpreted as 'winds.' For the great feast is the perfection of virtue. For this is also what the psalmist says: 'Hear the voice of rejoicing and confession of those celebrating' (Ps 100:1); for he who rejoices at the presence of the Spirit and confesses, not as one sinning and repenting, but as one giving thanks, celebrates—for the name of confession lies in place of thanksgiving, as in 'We confess to You, O Lord Father of the heavens...'

For they say, 'the thought of a man' [Eccl 2:2], which makes it clear that of the one rejoicing, 'he shall confess to you and a treasure of thought shall celebrate for you.' And he built there an altar to the Lord and called upon the name of the Lord.

Appropriately, the one who crossed over and upon the given mountain built the house of God; and having been illumined by the rising suns and having struck down the opposing things in such a way that no one would stir up indignation, he raised up an altar, upon which he completes the sacrifice of pleasingness and righteousness according to what was said before concerning the spiritual sacrifice, which is the system of virtues. 'And he called upon the name of the Lord,' which someone taking hastily might say means that the altar, which he built, he named 'of the Lord'; but it is possible to say it more mystically and more sublimely, that he called upon the name of the Lord not by a mere word, but truly, the mind making its petition to God, not performing the virtues through something else, but through the good itself. For according to this understanding, even the Savior, while teaching, instructed to pray and to say, 'Our Father,' not to do this by mere utterance, but so that they might present themselves as sons and no longer call upon God the Father in vain; thus we hear: 'No one says Lord Jesus except in the Holy Spirit' [1 Cor 12:3], and this does not apply to those who say this by mere utterance and in vain.

Therefore, Abraham was doing the building of the altar of virtues for the Lord, through it and not through something else. And Abram took [it] and having gone, he campaigned in the wilderness. Since the spoken word is not manifest, it must be spoken toward the understanding. For even if someone is perfect, he is not released from those who fight, even if he is a child, just as to the Corinthians, to whom Paul writes: 'You have not received a temptation which is not human; but God is faithful, who will not let you be tempted beyond what you are able, but with the temptation will make the way of the escape to endure' [1 Cor 10:13]. And to the Ephesians, as if already perfect, he writes and counts himself: 'For our struggle is not against blood and flesh' [Eph 6:12]; he does not say 'not...

title: The Famine and the Sojourning of Abraham
english: It has happened, but it is not our battle. For it once happened, when he set himself to be a fleshly thing having been brought under sin, signifying those in such a state, to whom it is also necessary to say as he himself writes: 'I beat my body and make it my slave, lest after preaching to others I myself become disqualified' (1 Cor 9:27). He fights with heavenly weapons against spiritual forces.

It is therefore perfect to fight just as Abraham stood at the house of God according to what was assigned, and by becoming like that himself, as it has been said: 'Those who have trusted in the Lord are like Mount Zion' (Ps 125:1). Having become thus, standing knowing that the opposing forces would not release him, he encamped, just as Jacob, when he was about to encounter Esau, a great war being present and envying him, 'saw the camp of God' (Gen 32:2); for it was necessary for God to be preparing for the athlete's courage to show him that he has allies.

And Elisha, when he was about to go out from the king of Syria, had a divine camp around himself, which the little boy of the prophet had been terrified by, later having become courageous from his eyes being opened. And likewise it is to have encamped 'in the wilderness.' So also the Savior is tested in the wilderness; and in Isaiah you have: 'As a storm through a wilderness, coming out of the wilderness from the earth' (Isa 34:10), which signifies a trial.

Therefore Abraham encamped 'in the wilderness'; for mostly the trials happened outside of cities because they were found without help from similar men: 'For brother helped by brother is like a strong city' (Prov 18:19). And the Savior, as foretold, is tested in the wilderness, so that what is called such may be: a soul in trial sees itself as a wilderness without allies, God does this providentially; for if he had pre-revealed to them the outcome and that they would conquer the trial, the effort would not have been great; nor did he send a prayer or do anything else. It is shown to them again that God also allies with them, so that they might not thus become evil. And so indeed for men, but for the Savior after the trial, angels appear, and these are for service, so that the ill-willed, before these angels appeared, might not say...

that victory belongs to angels. What is the service of the angels, or the placement of the souls who are persuaded by God? For they did not come for the sake of helping. And indeed he rebukes Peter because he wanted to fight excessively, saying: 'Do you think that I was not able to entreat my Father, and he would have given to me more than twelve legions of angels?' (Matt 26:53). Thus, an alliance is not necessary.

And there was a famine upon the earth; and Abram went down into Egypt to sojourn there, because a famine had grown strong upon the earth (Gen 12:10). The literal sense is clear; but this is the meaning for the intellect. The wise of God are above the earth, not being of it; therefore, in this way, a famine has occurred. For to those who think of earthly things, a famine of hearing the word of the Lord often happens, if they are worthy of it, and later they again receive it. In this way, too, Abram comes to 'sojourn' (not to dwell) in Egypt, descending in sympathy with those suffering the famine, not to live there; for those around Daniel did not come to Babylon because of sins, but so that they might help those deported there because of sins. For God has pity on those sinning to the extent that it is possible for them to repent. And just as doctors are sent where there is much harm or disease, not so that they themselves might share in the disease, but so that they might heal those who are sick, so the saints became present in the confusion and in Babylon, not being residents; for they had possessed nothing worthy of it, which is the property of those dwelling there.

And it happened, as Abram approached entering Egypt, that Abram said to Sarai his wife (Gen 12:11-13): 'I know that you are a woman of beautiful countenance; so it will be, when the Egyptians see you, they will say, "She is his wife," and they will kill me, and they will take you to themselves; so say then that you are my sister, so that it may go well for me because of you, and my soul may live because of you.' Regarding the spoken word, it is fitting with prudence, believing that God, having brought him out of his own land, will not neglect his marriage; he suggests to her to say to them that she is his sister, so that, this being said first and alone, they might not receive the notion that she is his wife, deceiving them through this.
